interactions.label: What best distinguishes dysentery from simple diarrhoea?

params.question: What best distinguishes dysentery from simple diarrhoea?

answers.text: High-volume watery stools caused by a secretory mechanism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: High-volume watery stools with a secretory mechanism characterise diarrhoea, not dysentery. In diarrhoea, excess water and salt are secreted into the bowel without tissue invasion.

answers.text: Bloody, mucoid stools with tenesmus due to mucosal invasion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Dysentery is defined by the presence of blood and mucus in stools, accompanied by tenesmus — a painful straining urge. This pattern indicates invasion and inflammation of the gut lining itself.

answers.text: Rapid onset of vomiting in several people after a shared meal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rapid onset with a common source exposure describes food poisoning, which is caused by ingesting food contaminated with germs or their preformed toxins.

answers.text: Frequent loose stools occurring more than three times per day

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Passing three or more loose stools per day is the definition of diarrhoea itself. Dysentery is specifically characterised by bloody, mucoid stools — not just increased frequency.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the key contrast: diarrhoea is secretory (watery, high volume, no blood), while dysentery is invasive (smaller volume, bloody, mucoid, with tenesmus and fever).
Well done! Dysentery is the invasive pattern — bloody and mucoid stools with tenesmus — in contrast to the watery, secretory pattern of simple diarrhoea.

params.question: What property of Shigella makes it far more contagious than Vibrio cholerae in person-to-person spread?

answers.text: Production of Shiga toxin that destroys enterocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Shiga toxin explains mucosal damage and bloody dysentery, but the toxin's destructive power does not determine the number of organisms needed to establish infection.

answers.text: Ability to invade through M-cells using actin rocketing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: M-cell invasion and actin rocketing explain how Shigella spreads within the colonic mucosa. This intracellular mechanism is separate from the question of how few organisms can initiate infection.

answers.text: An extremely low infective dose of only 10–100 organisms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Shigella can cause infection with as few as 10–100 organisms, compared to approximately 100 million organisms needed for cholera. This very low infective dose enables efficient person-to-person faeco-oral transmission, especially in crowded settings like schools.

answers.text: Formation of non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Colony morphology on culture media is a laboratory diagnostic feature used to identify Shigella. It has no bearing on contagiousness or the infective dose required to cause disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall that Shigella's infective dose is remarkably low — only 10–100 organisms — making it far more contagious than V. cholerae, which requires approximately 100 million organisms to cause infection.
Correct! The extremely low infective dose (10–100 organisms versus ~100 million for cholera) is why Shigella spreads so efficiently from person to person.

interactions.label: How does the urease enzyme of Helicobacter pylori contribute to its survival in

params.question: How does the urease enzyme of Helicobacter pylori contribute to its survival in the stomach?

answers.text: It directly damages gastric epithelial cells by punching pores in their membranes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pore formation in epithelial cells, causing them to swell and die, is the role of VacA toxin — not urease. VacA and urease have entirely different functions in pathogenesis.

answers.text: It disrupts tight junctions between cells and activates oncogenic signalling pathways

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Disruption of tight junctions and activation of cancer-promoting signals are the actions of CagA, not urease. CagA is injected into host cells and alters intracellular signalling.

answers.text: It neutralises gastric acid in the immediate surroundings of the bacterium, enabling colonisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Urease converts urea to ammonia, creating a local alkaline microenvironment that shields H. pylori from stomach acid and allows it to colonise the gastric antrum — the essential first step in pathogenesis.

answers.text: It serves as an adhesin that anchors the bacterium to the stomach lining

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adhesion to the gastric mucosa is mediated by specific adhesin proteins, not by urease. Urease and adhesins work in sequence: urease enables survival, then adhesins ensure attachment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: urease neutralises stomach acid, allowing H. pylori to survive. The tissue damage that causes ulcers comes from CagA (tight junction disruption) and VacA (pore formation) — not from urease itself.
Correct! Urease neutralises gastric acid around the bacterium, enabling H. pylori to colonise the gastric antrum — the essential first step before CagA and VacA cause tissue damage.

interactions.label: Why is HBeAg, rather than HBsAg, used as the specific marker of high infectivity

params.question: Why is HBeAg, rather than HBsAg, used as the specific marker of high infectivity in hepatitis B?

answers.text: HBsAg is present only in vaccinated individuals, not in those with active infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HBsAg is the hallmark marker of active hepatitis B infection, both acute and chronic. It is also the antigen used in the recombinant vaccine, but its presence in a patient always signals infection.

answers.text: HBeAg is a secreted form of the core antigen that specifically signals active viral replication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! HBeAg is produced from the core gene and secreted into the blood. Its presence specifically indicates that hepatitis B virus is actively replicating, making the patient highly infectious to others.

answers.text: HBsAg disappears early in acute infection, making it unreliable for assessing infectivity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HBsAg persists throughout active infection and remains positive for over six months in chronic carriers. It does not disappear early — though it can transiently clear during the window period.

answers.text: HBeAg is the primary target of antiviral drugs like tenofovir and entecavir

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antiviral drugs such as tenofovir and entecavir target the viral DNA polymerase with reverse transcriptase activity, not HBeAg. HBeAg serves as a monitoring marker, not a drug target.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall: HBeAg is a secreted form of the core antigen that signals active viral replication and high infectivity. HBsAg marks active infection, and antivirals target the DNA polymerase — each marker and target has a specific role.
Correct! HBeAg is the secreted core antigen product that specifically marks active viral replication and high infectivity — a distinct role from HBsAg, which marks infection itself.

interactions.label: A newborn is delivered to a mother who tested HBsAg-positive during pregnancy. W

params.question: A newborn is delivered to a mother who tested HBsAg-positive during pregnancy. What is the correct post-exposure prophylaxis for the baby?

answers.text: Hepatitis B vaccine alone at the standard birth dose within 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The birth dose alone initiates active immunity but does not provide the immediate passive protection needed to neutralise virus that may have been transmitted during delivery.

answers.text: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin alone, with vaccine deferred to the six-week visit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Immunoglobulin alone provides only temporary passive immunity without initiating the long-term active immune response that the vaccine generates. Both are needed together.

answers.text: Both hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the birth dose vaccine within 12 hours of birth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! A newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother requires both HBIG (for immediate passive immunity) and the birth dose vaccine (to begin active immunity), administered within 12 hours of birth to prevent vertical transmission.

answers.text: No immediate intervention; the pentavalent schedule beginning at six weeks provides adequate protection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Without immediate prophylaxis at birth, the risk of chronic hepatitis B from vertical transmission is very high. In India, mother-to-child transmission accounts for a large share of chronic carriers.

overallFeedback.feedback: For a newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother, both hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the birth dose vaccine must be given within 12 hours of birth — neither alone is sufficient to prevent vertical transmission.
Correct! Both HBIG and the birth dose vaccine within 12 hours are essential to prevent vertical transmission of hepatitis B from an infected mother.
